evidence.label: Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers
The Poisson-Dirichlet law for prime predecessors
Prime Predecessors with an Even Number of Prime Factors

headline: The prime factors of p − 1, for a random prime p, are claimed to split like a randomly broken stick.
scope: The law concerns the prime factors of p − 1 on a log scale, for primes p up to x chosen evenly.
plain: Pick a prime p at random and factor p − 1. Measure each prime factor by its share of the logarithm of p − 1. The second paper claims these shares follow the Poisson–Dirichlet law, the pattern of a stick broken at random points, as Ford, Konyagin and Luca conjectured. The first paper claims to prove Erdős's conjecture that some n are values of Euler's totient in nearly n ways. A third paper adds a parity result.
doesNot: This does not give rates of convergence, and it does not prove the independence assumptions used in models of prime chains.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: P. Erdős, who conjectured that some values of Euler's totient function are taken nearly n times
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims two named conjectures on shifted primes, one of Erdős and one of Ford, Konyagin and Luca.

explanation:
Take the prime 31. Then 31 − 1 = 30, which factors as 5 × 3 × 2. Measure each prime factor by its logarithm, divided by the logarithm of 30. The three shares come out near 0.473, 0.323 and 0.204. They add up to exactly 1, because the logarithms of the factors add up to the logarithm of 30. So the prime factors of p − 1 split a unit length into pieces.

For ordinary whole numbers chosen at random, the shape of this split has long been known. Dickman described the largest piece in 1930, and Billingsley found the joint law of the large pieces in 1972[3]. The answer is the Poisson–Dirichlet law (the paper calls it PD(1)). Here is a picture of it. Break a stick of length 1 at a uniformly random point and set one part aside. Break the rest the same way, again and again. Then sort the pieces from largest to smallest.

Primes are harder. Asking that a large number divides p − 1 puts p in a fixed pattern of remainders. Standard tools count primes in such patterns only when the number is below a fixed power of x[5]. But the full split involves products of factors right up to x. Ford, Konyagin and Luca conjectured in 2010 that p − 1 still follows PD(1)[2]. Before this, Bharadwaj and Rodgers had shown it only under an unproved hypothesis about primes in patterns[6].

The second paper claims that conjecture in full[2]. For a prime p chosen evenly up to x, the sorted shares converge to PD(1) as x grows[1]. That covers the largest share, the first two together, and any fixed number of them. One consequence concerns smooth predecessors, where every prime factor of p − 1 is small. It confirms Granville’s predicted share of primes p up to x with every prime factor of p − 1 at most x^(1/u)[7].

The first paper comes first in the chain of proofs. Fix any δ between 0 and 1/4. The paper claims at least x^(1 − o(1)) primes between 2x and 5x whose p − 1 has no prime factor above x^δ[10]. Here x^(1 − o(1)) means nearly x, up to a factor that grows slower than any power. Earlier work reached only smoothness thresholds near x^0.2961 and x^0.2844[17].

That input bears on Euler’s totient φ(m). It counts the numbers from 1 to m sharing no factor with m. Several m can give the same value. For example, φ(m) = 24 for exactly ten values of m. They are 35, 39, 45, 52, 56, 70, 72, 78, 84 and 90. Fix any ε > 0. The paper claims infinitely many n are hit by more than n^(1−ε) values of m[8]. If correct, this settles a conjecture of Erdős, recorded by Pomerance in 1980[9]. The exponent is the best possible, since the count can never exceed about n[9]. Earlier proven exponents were 0.7039 and then 0.7156[11,18].

A third paper claims infinitely many primes p of a special kind[12]. For them, p − 1 has no repeated prime factor and an even number of prime factors. Parity is a classic blind spot of sieve methods (ways of counting by removing multiples of small primes)[13]. It builds on the first paper’s tools[14].

The main new step in the second paper is a counting estimate for products of two parts[15]. The difficulty is that one side must carry marks recording chosen small prime factors of p − 1. The paper claims this works while the other side is only roughly controlled. The result is a limit law: it does not give how fast the limit is reached. It also does not prove the extra independence assumptions behind Ford, Konyagin and Luca’s prime-chain model[16].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. The three papers depend on each other. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the chain of three linked papers holds. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. The main law gives a limit without a rate.

glossary.meaning: For a prime p, the number p − 1 just before it.
The random way a stick of length 1 splits when you break it at random points again and again, with pieces sorted by size.
A number whose prime factors are all below a chosen limit.
φ(m), the count of numbers from 1 to m that share no factor with m.
All the numbers m that give the same totient value n.
A way of counting numbers with a property by removing multiples of small primes step by step.
